post1.text:
Most companies that stall between $50M and $500M don't have a strategy problem. They have a leadership problem they refuse to name.

Here's what that looks like in practice: A company adds senior executives to accelerate growth, as several fast-scaling firms have done recently, and within 18 months the new hires are either underperforming or gone. The business blamed fit. The real issue was that the existing leadership model couldn't support the weight of the company's next stage.

Three things scaling leaders consistently get wrong:

1. They hire for the job they have, not the company they're building.
2. They confuse adding headcount with building leadership capacity.
3. They wait for the org chart to break before redesigning how decisions get made.

Leadership at $50M works because of proximity. Leadership at $200M requires systems, trust, and the willingness to let go of control before you feel ready.

The question is not whether your team can execute today. It's whether your leadership model can survive your next stage of growth.

What has your company had to unlearn about leadership as it scaled?

post2.text:
A recent piece in HousingWire caught our attention. Buffini and Company just added three senior executives specifically to scale their coaching business. That's a deliberate, structured bet on leadership capacity as a growth lever.

Most companies at this stage do the opposite. They stretch existing leaders past their limits and wonder why execution slows down.

At Autobahn, we work with companies scaling from $50M to $500M and beyond. One pattern we see repeatedly: the businesses that scale cleanly are the ones that build leadership infrastructure ahead of demand, not in response to a crisis.

Buffini's move is a good signal. The question every growth-stage company should be asking right now is whether their leadership team is built for the company they are or the company they intend to become.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMicEFVX3lxTE80SmJLNXdFS1VDcE9QNXQ2YzNFUDNUSzItcWljNWEyb2NEUVJ0UzdweEIzaVZyclAyWk5fcW54Nlo2U21GSVVoMHFJaVpLSFdaMU1tMXRIWU8wMTJvc3RJNTM5VkhoaVFxZnZFM0VlWVU

post3.text:
When Buffini and Company added three senior executives to scale their coaching business, they made a leadership decision before a growth problem forced their hand. That distinction matters more than most leaders realize.

Chapter 1 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is titled Lead Like Lives Depend On It. Written by Katherine Slain, it opens with a premise that stops a lot of experienced leaders in their tracks: the leadership model that got your company to $50M is quietly working against you as you push toward $500M.

Katherine doesn't just name the problem. She lays out what it actually takes to lead through the uncomfortable space between those two numbers, where the old instincts mislead you and the new ones haven't been built yet.

If you're running a company in that range, this chapter was written for you.

Rock Your Business, the new book from Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most business owners optimize for revenue. The ones who actually win optimize for valuation multiples years before they ever talk to a buyer.

There is a fundamental difference between building a business and building a sellable asset. Entrepreneur.com recently highlighted how founders who wait until they want to exit to think about exit strategy are already behind. That tracks with what we see at the $50M to $500M level every day.

Three things that move your multiple more than top-line growth ever will:

1. Revenue quality matters more than revenue size. Recurring, contracted, and diversified revenue commands premium multiples. Lumpy, customer-concentrated revenue destroys them.

2. EBITDA margin trends tell buyers whether your growth is sustainable or manufactured. A rising margin story is worth more than a flat one at higher absolute numbers.

3. Operational dependency on the founder is a silent multiple killer. If the business cannot run without you for 90 days, buyers will price that risk accordingly.

So here is the question worth sitting with: If a buyer evaluated your business today, what would they see that you have been choosing not to fix?

#MergersAndAcquisitions #BusinessValuation #ScalingUp

post2.text:
A recent piece from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce walks through the fundamentals of building an exit strategy, and it is worth a read for any business owner thinking about what comes next.

What the article does well is frame the exit as a planning decision, not a reactive one. What it does not address is what this looks like specifically for companies in the $50M to $500M range, where the stakes, the complexity, and the buyer universe are fundamentally different from a small business sale.

At that scale, your exit strategy is not a checklist. It is a years-long positioning process that shapes how you hire, structure deals, manage customer relationships, and report financials.

If you are running a business at that level and have not stress-tested your exit readiness, now is the time to start.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMihAFBVV95cUxONERpMjFwUjkzVW8xLTRScUhVWTQ5VUFMS1R5cFY4c2p2eXYzZ3NYc0V0NUlaMmREUXM2N3VSaThYUjhERGNiSmhFTDB5TVBYNEhrOU9WSHRyYThWWUlUY2RYNlVFNkhvVGU4V3h1bXAtVzUwVVh0bG5FOWxmTUNJTTBJYjI

post3.text:
Silicon Valley Bank recently published a breakdown of exit strategies, covering when founders should sell and when they should hold. It is a solid framework for thinking about timing.

But timing is only one piece of the puzzle. The deeper question is whether your business is actually positioned to command the multiple it deserves when that moment arrives.

Chapter 2 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles exactly this. Titled 'Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit' and authored by Paul Belair and George Hohman, it goes beyond timing to show leaders at the $50M to $500M level how the decisions they make today are either building or eroding enterprise value right now.

One thing the chapter makes clear: the highest multiples are not earned at the closing table. They are earned in the three to five years before anyone ever makes an offer.

post1.text:
Most strategic plans fail not because the strategy was wrong, but because the organization was never actually built to execute it.

Leaders at growing companies spend months crafting a compelling vision, then hand it off to managers who are still running the same processes they used when the company was half the size. The gap between strategy and execution is not an ideas problem. It is a structure problem.

Recent reporting from Supply Chain Management Review reinforces this: the C-suite often operates in separate lanes, each optimizing for their own function while the company-wide strategy stalls out in the middle.

Three things scaling companies almost always get wrong:

1. They treat annual planning as a one-time event instead of a living system.
2. They promote operators into strategy roles without equipping them for the transition.
3. They measure activity instead of outcomes, then wonder why targets slip.

If your leadership team cannot describe your top three priorities in the same words, your strategy is not a strategy. It is a wish list.

What does execution actually look like inside your organization right now?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Supply Chain Management Review made a sharp observation: when C-suite leaders are not aligned on how strategy translates into day-to-day decisions, execution breaks down at the enterprise level, not the frontline.

For companies scaling past $50M, this is one of the most expensive blind spots in the building.

At Autobahn, we see it constantly. Leadership teams that are deeply aligned on vision but completely misaligned on who owns what, by when, and how success gets measured. Strategy documents gather dust while the business runs on habit.

Alignment is not a culture initiative. It is an operational discipline, and it requires a system, not a retreat.

If your leadership team is navigating this gap, this article is worth five minutes of your time.

post3.text:
Strategy without execution is a hobby. That is the core tension Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall tackle in Chapter 3 of Rock Your Business, titled What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes.

The chapter draws on real business experience across industries that look nothing alike on the surface but share the same underlying challenge: how do you build a planning and execution system that actually holds as your company scales?

One insight that hits differently when you read it in context: the companies that scale successfully are not the ones with the best strategies on paper. They are the ones that figured out how to make strategic priorities visible and accountable at every level of the organization, week in and week out.

The framework Rafa and Jim share is practical, field-tested, and built for leaders running companies between $50M and $500M.

post1.text:
Most $50M+ companies don't have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit.

There's a difference. A habit is what your team does because it worked before. A strategy is what you've deliberately designed to work at the next level of scale.

Recent research from McKinsey confirms what we see constantly with our clients: the threshold for sustainable B2B growth has shifted upward. Companies that treat revenue as a byproduct of relationships and referrals are increasingly getting outpaced by competitors who have engineered repeatable, deliberate growth systems.

Here's what that means practically for leaders at your stage:

1. Your close rate is not a sales metric. It's a strategy diagnostic.
2. If your top rep leaving would materially hurt revenue, you don't have a sales engine. You have a dependency.
3. Market share in your core segment should be a number you can state confidently, not estimate loosely.

So here's the real question: If your best salesperson took a six-month sabbatical tomorrow, would your revenue plan survive?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Bain and Company breaks down what separates B2B companies that consistently win new customers from those that grow in bursts and stall. Their finding is worth sitting with: top-performing companies treat new customer acquisition as a repeatable system, not a series of heroic individual efforts.

At Autobahn, we see this play out constantly with companies scaling through the $50M to $500M range. The moment growth becomes dependent on a handful of rainmakers instead of a defined process, you've introduced fragility at exactly the wrong time.

If your sales motion isn't something you can train, measure, and hand off, it isn't a strategy. It's a personality.

Read the full Bain piece and ask yourself whether your team is building a machine or relying on magic.

post3.text:
New research from McKinsey on B2B growth confirms something Deb and Brandon write about directly in Chapter 4 of our upcoming book.

The chapter is called "Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation." The title is not an exaggeration.

What Deb and Brandon found working with scaling companies is that most leaders in the $50M to $500M range believe they have a sales strategy because they have a sales team. Those are not the same thing. One produces activity. The other produces predictable, compounding revenue growth.

Chapter 4 lays out what it actually takes to build a sales strategy that scales with your organization instead of breaking under the weight of it. One piece of it will make you rethink how you're currently allocating your top sales talent.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling people get when they interact with your company, and most $50M+ businesses have no idea what that feeling actually is.

Ulta's CMO recently spoke about how they think about brand building across every customer touchpoint, not just paid media. That kind of intentional, integrated thinking is rare, and it separates companies that scale from companies that stall.

Here is what mid-market leaders consistently get wrong about branding:

1. They treat marketing as a department, not a function that runs through every part of the business. Sales, service, operations, all of it shapes the brand.

2. They confuse activity with strategy. Posting content and running ads is not a brand. A clear position that makes the right customers choose you over everyone else, that is a brand.

3. They build for today's revenue, not tomorrow's market. Brand equity is a long-term asset. Treat it like one.

If a stranger walked into your company tomorrow with no context, what would they smell? What impression would stick?

What does your brand actually communicate when no one is watching?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Adweek broke down how Campari keeps its portfolio of heritage brands culturally relevant across generations without losing what made those brands iconic in the first place.

For companies scaling past $50M, this is a real tension. Growth pressure pushes leaders to chase trends and broaden appeal. But brand dilution is one of the fastest ways to commoditize a business that once had a distinct identity.

The Campari approach is worth studying. They protect the core story while finding new contexts where that story lands. That is not a marketing tactic. It is a strategic discipline.

If you are scaling and feeling the pull to reinvent your brand to reach new markets, pause. The question is not how to change your brand. It is how to extend it without breaking it.

Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiuwFBVV95cUxOME5NSGZueEQtNEplYmN2bWt2NHBnYWlPNEM3Wm5JYnhlMzNxSGpiRkxhN1NmVVh2UnVFa0dXTG1rNFA3d05RdkRNcUkxcGlaMVRSTklhZDFpVkttRVN1SFFGY2lVRDRncTQ3WXQwYkx3NW55MHdiTGlYVlN0ZXBJa0NtYjVCa21FOFF6eFNFYVZPcVFyTk91OG5rZ2FRX1M0MnNvalZFQW1PVXBUZDJIcmFaSlMtUFJkVFZz

post3.text:
Campari has spent decades keeping iconic brands alive by staying intentional about what those brands stand for and how they show up in culture. It sounds simple. It is not.

Chapter 5 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is titled 'What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?' Authors Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West tackle exactly this challenge for scaling companies. The chapter pushes leaders to get honest about whether their brand has a distinct identity or just a presence.

One of the sharpest insights in the chapter: most companies at this stage are marketing louder without getting clearer. More spend, more channels, more content, but no stronger signal. That is a growth ceiling hiding in plain sight.

If your marketing could be swapped with a competitor's without anyone noticing, that is the problem to solve first.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost.

Most companies scaling past $50M default to headcount as the answer to every operational problem. It feels decisive. It looks like progress. But SHRM's latest research on 2026 hiring trends makes something clear: the companies winning on talent are hiring with precision, not volume. They know exactly what gap they are filling before the job post goes live.

Here is what that means in practice for scaling companies:

1. Every open role should map to a specific revenue or operational outcome. If you cannot name it, you are not ready to hire.

2. Speed-to-productivity matters more than speed-to-hire. A fast bad hire costs you six to twelve months.

3. Your talent process is a signal to your best candidates. Disorganized hiring tells them exactly how you operate.

Growth exposes every weakness in your people strategy. The organizations that scale well treat talent acquisition as a system, not a reaction.

What is the last role you hired for, and did you know exactly why before you posted it?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SHRM, titled 'Precision Over Scale: The New Rules of Hiring in 2026,' challenges something most growing companies still get wrong.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly with companies in the $50M to $200M range. They treat hiring like a volume problem. Open seats feel urgent, so speed becomes the priority, and rigor goes out the window.

The SHRM piece reframes this well. The best talent teams in 2026 are slowing down the front end of hiring so they can accelerate everything that comes after it. Role clarity, outcome alignment, and structured evaluation are not bureaucracy. They are the difference between a team that scales and one that stalls.

If your hiring process was built when you were half your current size, it is already costing you. Read the full piece and ask your leadership team whether your talent engine is built for where you are going.

The Talent Engine, written by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West, is built for leaders who have outgrown their original people strategy and do not yet have the structure to replace it. That gap is where most scaling companies lose their best people and their momentum.

One thing the chapter makes clear: the talent problems you face at $100M are not bigger versions of your $30M problems. They are different problems entirely. And they require a different kind of thinking, not just more HR resources.

If your people strategy is still running on instinct and institutional memory, this chapter will change how you see it.

post1.text:
More metrics will not save your business. They will bury it.

Most leadership teams at the $50M+ level are not suffering from a lack of data. They are suffering from an addiction to it. When every department reports 15 KPIs to the executive team, nobody is actually managing anything. Everyone is just watching numbers move.

A recent NetSuite analysis on real estate performance tracking illustrates this well. Even in a data-rich industry, the firms that perform best are not the ones tracking the most metrics. They are the ones that have ruthlessly chosen which numbers actually predict outcomes versus which numbers just describe what already happened.

Three things worth considering for any scaling business:

1. Lag indicators tell you history. Lead indicators let you change the future. Most dashboards are almost entirely lag.
2. If your team cannot recite your top five KPIs from memory, you have too many.
3. Accountability breaks down when ownership of a metric is shared by more than one person.

What would your team cut if you could only keep five metrics?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Business.com rounded up 14 tools for tracking KPIs across business functions. Useful list. But here is what it cannot tell you: the tool is never the problem.

At Autobahn, we work with companies scaling from $50M toward $500M. Almost none of them have a technology gap when it comes to metrics. What they have is a clarity gap. Leaders add tracking tools the same way they add KPIs: assuming more visibility creates more accountability. It rarely does.

Before your team evaluates another dashboard or reporting platform, ask one question first: does every person on our leadership team know exactly which two or three numbers they personally own and move each week?

If the answer is no, a new tool will not fix that. Start there.

https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMingFBVV95cUxQcWNPSTVTUDVYYURoVkZKa0ItNEtQbmJqWlNJTlIzUVZqclAxMHFaajNobC1JbGNkZGZVajN6MWJLT1pJcXktVG10VG8zUUljdU43NU5WR1cyNDB4QkxONlJkb3hJR2FfNzdGZHd1VWhPbTktdU1vdTEzamFWY2ZFVDNKUFIwRG91ZDdWU1UyN2twNFpLd1JjU3EzTUpjdw?oc=5

post3.text:
Hootsuite recently published a breakdown of 31 social media KPIs worth tracking in 2026. Thirty-one. For one channel.

This is exactly the problem that Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall tackle in Chapter 7 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond.

The chapter is titled Death by KPIs for a reason. The authors work with leadership teams who have built sophisticated reporting systems that have somehow made decision-making slower, not faster. The insight that hits hardest: tracking more metrics is often a form of organizational avoidance. It feels like rigor while masking a fear of real accountability.

There is a framework in this chapter that will change how your leadership team selects, assigns, and reviews performance data. We will leave the details for the book.

Rock Your Business -- available soon. Follow us for updates.

Here is what high-growth companies do differently.

articles.snippet: What is Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Business?  IBM

post1.text:
Most companies are failing at AI not because they lack the technology, but because they lack the discipline to use it well.

Forbes recently compiled a sweeping look at AI adoption trends heading into 2026. The numbers tell a story that most executives do not want to hear: investment is surging while measurable productivity gains remain elusive for the majority of organizations.

Here is what that means for leaders running $50M+ businesses:

1. Buying AI tools is not an AI strategy. Without clear ownership and defined use cases, you are funding chaos at scale.

2. The companies pulling ahead are treating AI like any other operational capability: they assign accountability, measure outputs, and iterate fast.

3. Speed of adoption matters less than depth of integration. A focused deployment in one department outperforms scattered rollouts across ten.

The gap between AI hype and AI results is a leadership problem, not a technology problem.

So here is the question worth sitting with: Is your organization actually using AI, or just paying for it?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune dropped a number worth pausing on: 90% of executives say AI has not boosted productivity, yet layoffs tied to AI are still happening.

That combination should concern every scaling company.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern often. Leaders cut headcount expecting AI to absorb the workload, but without redesigning the workflows around it, they just end up with less capacity and no efficiency gain.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this is a critical window. You have enough complexity to benefit enormously from AI, and enough agility to implement it correctly before bad habits calcify.

The fix is not more AI spend. It is better thinking about where human judgment ends and automation begins.

Read the full Fortune piece here and ask yourself whether your AI rollout is built on strategy or assumption: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMifEFVX3lxTE5LZWF5Vkc3Wk9DVVd5aE83ZGVhbWMyb3U3MW1kcHljOHdwcjdjTmt1SmU5bFVRblVaZGJsRndNRS1fWExxc3IyZDBJcnlxZHhYVUFhV1pBSzVRS0R1RVJlNVYxM0pzRXZKcG96RExTdTVlMnhBWDNMUlVuUGM

In Chapter 8 of Rock Your Business, titled The Third Monitor Theory, Hudson Shank and Jonathan Slain dig into exactly why well-funded AI initiatives stall inside growing companies. The chapter introduces a framework for thinking about where AI actually fits inside your operation versus where leaders assume it fits.

The distinction sounds subtle. The revenue impact is not.

If your team is running AI tools without a clear theory for how they connect to business outcomes, Chapter 8 was written for you.

post1.text:
The leaders most likely to stall your company's growth are not the ones who lack confidence. They are the ones who fake it so convincingly that they stop learning.

Imposter syndrome gets treated like a weakness to eliminate. But research consistently shows that leaders who experience it are often more self-aware, more coachable, and more accurate in assessing their own gaps. SmartBrief recently covered how that internal discomfort, when redirected, becomes a driver of genuine growth rather than a liability.

For leaders scaling a business past $50M, here is what that actually means in practice:

First, the feeling of being out of your depth is a signal that your role has outgrown your old playbook. That is not failure. That is evidence of progress.

Second, the executives who perform best at this stage are not the ones who have eliminated self-doubt. They are the ones who have built enough self-knowledge to act decisively in spite of it.

Third, suppressing imposter syndrome pushes it underground, where it shows up as micromanagement, risk aversion, and poor delegation.

So here is the real question: Is your leadership team naming what they feel, or just performing certainty?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Seattle University outlines six practical ways leaders can overcome imposter syndrome when stepping into a new role. The advice is solid, and it applies well beyond first-time executives.

At Autobahn, we see this play out constantly with companies scaling past $50M. The leadership identity that got you here rarely matches the one the next stage of growth demands. That gap between who you were and who the business now needs you to be is where imposter syndrome lives.

The companies that scale well do not wait for their leaders to feel ready. They build cultures and coaching structures that help leaders grow into the role in real time.

If your senior team is quietly struggling with this, it is worth a direct conversation.

Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business is titled "How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?" and it asks one of the most honest questions in the book.

Authored by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo, this chapter tackles something most leadership books skip entirely: what happens psychologically when a founder or executive arrives at a level of success they never fully believed they would reach.

The insight that stopped us in our tracks is this: imposter syndrome at the $50M to $500M stage is not about doubting your past. It is about not yet having a clear identity for who you need to become next. That distinction changes everything about how you address it.

This is not a chapter about feeling better. It is a chapter about leading better.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

Here is what high-growth leaders actually do about it.

post1.text:
Most founders spend years building a business they never actually designed their life around.

That gap is expensive. Not just financially.

A recent Entrepreneur.com piece pointed out something most growth-stage founders already know but rarely act on: exit planning gets treated as a finance exercise, not a life design decision. By the time the numbers line up, the personal vision is an afterthought.

If you are running a $50M+ company, here is what that actually costs you:

1. You optimize the business for a buyer, not for the life you want post-close. Those are rarely the same target.

2. Work-life design gets deferred indefinitely. There is always a next milestone. The deferral becomes permanent.

3. Your team mirrors your behavior. Leaders who never come up for air build cultures that burn people out and lose talent at scale.

Life planning is not a soft topic. It is a strategic one. The founders who scale well are the ones who get deliberate about what they are actually building toward.

What does your business look like if you design it around your life first, not last?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Deutsche Bank Wealth Management tackled the wealth planning questions entrepreneurs face after selling a business. The timing, the liquidity decisions, the identity shift. It is a smart read.

But here is what it does not cover: most founders at the $50M to $500M stage are not ready for that conversation because they never did the life planning work before the exit.

At Autobahn, we see this consistently. The financial plan is polished. The personal vision is blank.

Scaling a company without a clear picture of what you are scaling toward is how founders end up cash-rich and directionless at the finish line.

If you are serious about building something you can actually exit well, start with the life design work now, not after close.

Read the full Deutsche Bank piece here: https://news.google.

post3.text:
Entrepreneur.com recently published a candid piece on how founders plan obsessively for growth but almost never plan for the exit. The insight lands hard if you have lived it.

Chapter 10 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, addresses exactly this. The chapter is called Coming Up for Air, written by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain.

The premise is straightforward: at a certain scale, the cost of not designing your life intentionally is higher than any operational inefficiency you are trying to fix. Founders who reach $100M, $200M, $500M without doing this work do not suddenly figure it out at the finish line.

Chapter 10 gives leaders a concrete way to think about life planning as part of the growth strategy, not separate from it.

There is one reframe in that chapter that changes how most executives think about their calendar entirely. We will leave it there for now.

Rock Your Business -- available soon. Follow us for updates.

Almost none of them have written down what they actually want their life to look like at $200M or at the close of a deal. That gap is not a personal failure. It is a planning failure. And it compounds quietly until it is very loud.
